companies.name: Evalueserve

leaders.name: Nitin Narkhede
leaders.role: Chief Technology Officer (appointed July 2026, ex-Wipro Lab45)

companies.business: A global "knowledge process" company — big corporations (banks, pharma firms, law firms) pay them to do research, data analysis and reporting that would otherwise need a large in-house team. Their pitch, "Mind+Machine," blends 5,000+ human subject-matter experts with AI tools, so clients get analyst-quality work at software speed. That mix of skilled people + AI is what sets them apart from plain offshore outsourcing shops.
risks: Sits on extremely sensitive client data — unpublished financial models, M&A research, drug pipeline data — a leak hurts their Fortune-1000 clients too.
A brand-new CEO plus a newly appointed CTO (July 2026) means a broader leadership handover than usual — exactly the moment where access rights and departing-staff accounts need cleaning up.
Research analysts are highly mobile talent, regularly hired away by rival research/KPO firms and the Big 4 — each exit is a potential data walkout.
companies.money: Private company — profit isn't published. Third-party estimates put revenue around $1.2 billion company-wide, with staff growing from roughly 4,500 to over 6,000 in recent years.
companies.ai: AI is the whole business model, not a side project. The CEO joined from Google Cloud's AI/data partnerships team, and the new CTO (July 2026) previously ran Wipro's AI innovation lab (Lab45) — both hires point to an even harder push on AI adoption, internally and for clients.

companies.name: SirionLabs

leaders.name: Ajay Agrawal
leaders.note: Direct LinkedIn not confirmed — search "Ajay Agrawal SirionLabs".

leaders.name: Aditya Gupta, Claude Marais, Kanti Prabha

companies.business: Sells software that helps very large companies manage their contracts — not just storing them, but using AI to read every contract, flag risky clauses, and track obligations. Named a Gartner "Leader" in this category four years running; their AI is trained on more than 32 million real contracts, a meaningful edge over simple e-signature or document-storage tools.
risks: The entire product runs on other companies' most confidential commercial contracts (pricing, IP terms, M&A deals) — a very attractive theft target.
Acquired by private equity firm Haveli Investments in January 2026 — ownership changes often bring restructuring and staff turnover, a classic window for data walking out the door.
As a software vendor plugged into many enterprise systems, a breach here could ripple into all of their customers ("supply-chain" risk).
companies.money: Private company. Reported revenue grew from about $54 million (2023) to about $85 million (2024) — roughly 57% growth. Valued near $1 billion before the 2026 acquisition.
companies.ai: AI isn't an add-on — their product is built on generative AI plus proprietary models. Responsible AI/data handling is core to their credibility with enterprise customers.

companies.name: KRBL Limited
companies.employeeBand: Employee count not disclosed to us

leaders.name: Anoop Kumar Gupta, Arun Kumar Gupta
CTO
leaders.role: Not applicable in the traditional sense — likely a Head of IT

companies.business: The company behind "India Gate" basmati rice — the world's largest basmati rice miller and exporter. What sets them apart is controlling the whole chain: sourcing paddy from farmers, milling, branding, and exporting worldwide, rather than just trading rice. Full control over quality is their brand promise.
risks: Sourcing data, farmer/quality records and export pricing are commercially sensitive — costly if lost to a competitor.
Rice mills increasingly run on connected industrial equipment — a newer, often under-protected attack surface.
They've already bought Data Leak Prevention for web traffic, showing awareness — but it doesn't yet cover email or endpoints.
companies.money: Listed company — figures are public. Revenue: ₹5,341 cr (FY23) → ₹5,365 cr (FY24) → ₹5,594 cr (FY25), slow steady growth. But profit has been falling: ₹701 cr (FY23) → ₹596 cr (FY24) → ₹476 cr (FY25) — real margin pressure. Their most recent quarter (Q1 FY27, reported August 2026) showed a sharp rebound: consolidated net profit jumped 73% year-on-year to ₹261 cr, even as revenue dipped 6% (fewer rice exports, offset by strong domestic sales) — margins expanded significantly.
companies.ai: The wider agri/FMCG sector is starting to use AI for demand forecasting and computer-vision rice quality grading — useful, but not yet a headline transformation for KRBL specifically.

companies.name: Nykaa (FSN E-Commerce Ventures)

leaders.name: CTO
leaders.role: No formally titled "CTO" found publicly — worth confirming

companies.business: India's leading beauty and personal-care e-commerce platform, plus fashion (Nykaa Fashion) and its own manufactured beauty brands. Unlike a plain marketplace, Nykaa differentiates on curated, trusted product selection, strong physical stores, and content/influencer-driven shopping — plus owning some of the brands it sells, improving margins.
risks: This isn't hypothetical: customers publicly complained (2021–2024) about scam calls referencing exact order details, and a 2024 leak at a third-party marketing vendor ("Gamooga") exposed Nykaa customer data along with other major Indian brands.
Shows their vendor/partner ecosystem is a real weak point, not just their own systems.
Millions of customers' personal and payment details make them a constant fraud/phishing target.
companies.money: Listed company — figures are public and strong. Revenue: ₹7,058 cr (FY23) → ₹9,055 cr (FY24) → ₹11,775 cr (FY25), growing ~24%/year. Profit improved faster than revenue — up roughly 81% year-on-year in FY25. Momentum has continued: Q1 FY27 (quarter to June 2026, reported August 2026) revenue grew 29% year-on-year to ₹2,782 cr and net profit more than tripled to ₹80 cr, with the Nykaa Fashion business turning close-to-profitable for the first time.
companies.ai: Investing in AI for personalised shopping recommendations, virtual try-on features, and demand/inventory forecasting — standard for a modern e-commerce leader.

companies.name: Mother Dairy

leaders.name: Leadership in transition
leaders.role: MD Manish Bandlish stepped down 30 Nov 2025; Deputy MD overseeing operations. Some reports cite Jayatheertha Chary as successor — confirm before referencing externally.

leaders.name: CTO
leaders.role: Not publicly named — likely a Head of IT/Digital role

companies.business: The trusted Delhi-NCR household name for milk, plus the "Dhara" edible-oil brand and "Safal" fruit & vegetables. Operates as a subsidiary linked to the National Dairy Development Board (NDDB), blending a farmer-welfare, cooperative-style mission with private-company operations — that government-linked trust factor is a big part of its brand strength.
risks: A very recent, high-level leadership exit (the MD) is exactly the moment old access rights and accounts need reviewing and closing off properly.
Cold-chain and processing plants increasingly rely on connected equipment — an under-protected area for most FMCG/dairy players.
A large distributor and vendor network means sensitive supply and pricing data regularly travels outside their own walls.
companies.money: Private (NDDB-linked) — profit isn't disclosed, but turnover is: ₹15,037 cr (FY24) → ₹17,500 cr (FY25) → a targeted ₹20,300 cr in FY26 (~17% growth) — a genuinely strong growth run.
companies.ai: The dairy/FMCG sector broadly is starting to use AI for demand forecasting, dynamic pricing and predicting spoilage/wastage — relevant, but not yet a headline story specifically for Mother Dairy.

companies.name: Axtria
companies.sector: AI & Data Analytics for Life Sciences/Pharma
companies.business: Builds cloud software and AI/data platforms specifically for pharmaceutical and life-sciences companies — helping them plan sales territories, forecast drug demand, and run commercial operations more effectively. Being laser-focused on life sciences (rather than generic analytics for anyone) is exactly what sets them apart.
risks: Handles commercially sensitive pharma sales data and patient-adjacent data for clients across 75+ countries — a high regulatory bar.
Their own CEO is publicly pushing the industry toward "agentic AI" (AI that takes action, not just gives answers) — raising the stakes on getting underlying data governance right first.
companies.money: Private company — exact profit not published. Estimated revenue around $105 million ARR, with a valuation reportedly above $1 billion. Staff grew from ~4,718 (2024) to ~4,826 (2025).
companies.ai: AI is their whole strategy right now. In June 2026 they hosted "Axtria Ignite 2026," gathering 450+ life sciences executives around "Industrializing Intelligence: The Agentic Enterprise." CEO Jassi Chadha's own message: "fix the foundation before you scale AI" — don't rush AI agents without solid data quality and governance first. In August 2026 they announced plans to grow their specialist "Forward Deployed Engineering" team — engineers who pair pharma expertise with AI engineering — to 1,000 people by the end of 2026, underlining how central hands-on AI deployment has become to their business.

companies.name: Shardul Amarchand Mangaldas & Co

leaders.name: Pallavi Shroff & Akshay Chudasama
leaders.note: No confirmed direct LinkedIn found. No conventional CTO role.

companies.business: One of India's largest full-service law firms (169 partners, 834 lawyers), handling major corporate deals, mergers and disputes for large companies. Formed from the 2015 split of the old Amarchand Mangaldas firm. Scale and a top-tier corporate/M&A practice set it apart.
risks: Very well documented: partners regularly move between SAM and rival firm Khaitan & Co (and others) — most recently a senior partner and two colleagues left SAM for Khaitan in 2026. Every move risks client files, deal knowledge and contacts leaving with the person.
Law firms sit on market-moving information (undisclosed M&A deals) — a high-value target for cybercriminals and even insider trading schemes.
companies.money: Private partnership — Indian law firms don't publish financial results, so no reliable figures are available publicly.
companies.ai: Legal AI tools are cutting research time 30–50% industry-wide, but adoption is early — only ~20–27% of Indian law firms use sophisticated AI tools today, and most CEOs say they don't yet trust AI without strong governance. As a market leader, SAM is very likely evaluating these tools.

companies.name: Khaitan & Co

leaders.name: Haigreve Khaitan
leaders.note: No confirmed direct LinkedIn found. No formal CTO role identified.

companies.business: Often ranked India's largest full-service law firm, founded in 1911 — one of the oldest continuously operating firms in the country. Covers corporate law, tax, IP and disputes, and has historically grown aggressively by hiring senior lawyers away from rival firms.
risks: The same lateral-hiring dynamic as SAM applies in reverse too — partners and their client relationships move in and out of Khaitan regularly, each move a potential data walkout.
Just opened a new Hyderabad office (2026) with four new leaders — new offices mean new local IT setups and endpoints to secure from day one.
companies.money: Private partnership — no publicly available revenue or profit figures.
companies.ai: Same industry-wide shift as SAM — legal AI adoption accelerating for research and drafting, with governance and client-confidentiality still catching up.

companies.name: Indian Energy Exchange (IEX)
companies.business: Runs India's largest online marketplace for buying and selling electricity — generators and big buyers (utilities, industries) trade electricity, green energy and carbon certificates in real time. Being the first mover with roughly 85%+ of India's power-trading volume makes them the dominant player — essentially critical national infrastructure.
risks: As literal national trading infrastructure, IEX is a textbook target for state-level or highly sophisticated attackers — a disruption here could ripple into India's actual power supply/demand matching.
Government scrutiny of critical infrastructure cybersecurity (CERT-In, NCIIPC) is intensifying — a company regulators expect to be a role model on security.
Only ~300 staff run this national platform — a lean team almost certainly leans heavily on external vendors for security.
companies.money: Listed company — figures are public. Revenue: ₹474 cr (FY23) → ₹449 cr (FY24, a dip) → ₹657 cr (FY25, back to strong growth). Profit: ₹305 cr (FY23) → ₹351 cr (FY24) → ₹429 cr (FY25) — healthy and growing. Growth continued into FY27: Q1 FY27 (quarter to June 2026) revenue was up 11% year-on-year to ₹158 cr and profit up 12% to ₹134 cr, driven by record electricity-trading volumes during a hot summer.
companies.ai: Power exchanges increasingly use AI/ML for demand and price forecasting — because it feeds a live financial trading market, model accuracy and integrity really matter.

companies.name: Sterlite Power
companies.business: Builds high-voltage electricity transmission lines and infrastructure in India and Brazil, often transferring finished projects into infrastructure investment trusts (like IndiGrid) for long-term ownership. Effectively pioneered the model of private companies building India's power transmission network — a role that used to sit only with government bodies. In a 2025–26 corporate restructuring, the group renamed its transmission-and-manufacturing business "Sterlite Electric Limited" and moved its build-operate-transfer infrastructure projects into a separate entity (Sterlite Grid 5) — worth knowing when confirming exactly which legal entity we're dealing with.
risks: Power transmission runs on industrial control systems (substations, grid control software) — often less protected than regular office IT.
Operates across two countries (India and Brazil), meaning data crosses borders and multiple regulatory regimes.

The renamed Sterlite Electric Limited filed IPO paperwork with SEBI in September 2025, but in 2026 said it was withdrawing that filing due to market volatility — this kind of restructuring and on-again/off-again IPO planning is typically a higher-risk window for security, with new entities, new IT setups and reshuffled access rights.
companies.money: Privately held (unlisted) — one estimate puts FY24 revenue around ₹7,516 crore, but as an unlisted company this isn't officially audited/public the way listed-company numbers are — treat as approximate.
companies.ai: The power/grid sector is starting to use AI to predict equipment failures before they happen and for weather-based load forecasting — growing, but not yet headline news for Sterlite Power specifically.

companies.name: R Systems International
companies.business: Majority-owned by Blackstone, R Systems builds software products and platforms for global clients in telecom, healthcare and banking, and runs business-process services. Unlike a typical staffing/outsourcing company, they focus on actually engineering products — and notably, are building out their own cybersecurity services line, worth knowing when we talk to them.
risks: As an IT services company, they hold source code, infrastructure access and data for many client companies — a breach could cascade into their whole client base ("supply-chain" risk).
Engineers' laptops and dev environments are a high-value target since that's where client IP actually lives day to day.
companies.money: Listed company. Recent full-year figures show revenue around ₹2,230 crore and profit around ₹193 crore, with Q4 profit alone up 40% year-on-year — a strong, improving trend. That momentum has accelerated further: Q2 2026 revenue crossed ₹600 crore for the first time (up 30% year-on-year), and profit for the first half of 2026 was up over 50% year-on-year.
companies.ai: AI is central to their current pitch — their latest annual report is literally titled "Where AI Meets Human Experience," reflecting a deliberate repositioning around AI-augmented engineering and delivery.

companies.name: S&A Law Offices

leaders.name: Daizy Chawla & Gunita Pahwa
leaders.note: No confirmed direct LinkedIn found. No CTO role — typical for a firm this size.

companies.business: A mid-size, full-service Indian law firm with offices in Delhi, Gurgaon, Mumbai and Bengaluru (300+ legal professionals), with a strong heritage in intellectual property (IP/patent) work alongside general corporate and dispute practice. Being nimbler and more specialised than the mega-firms is their differentiator.
risks: They handle clients' IP filings and patent data — commercially very sensitive competitive intelligence for those clients if it ever leaked.
As a mid-size firm, likely a smaller dedicated security budget/team than the mega-firms, so each client matter may carry relatively higher exposure.
India's new DPDP Act (finalised November 2025) applies to them too — even smaller firms are now formal "data fiduciaries" with legal security obligations.
companies.money: Private partnership — no publicly available revenue or profit figures.
companies.ai: Same broader legal-AI wave affecting all Indian law firms — smaller firms often adopt cheap, easy-to-access AI tools quickly, sometimes with less formal oversight, which is worth flagging.
